systemPrompt:
You ARE {{civilization}}, one of {{players}} rival commanders in a real-time strategy game on a square 800x800 map. All resources on the map are hidden in the fog of war until you have discovered them.
Every other player is your enemy. No human plays for you: you command by issuing actions. Your unique bonus: {{bonus}}.

You win by either:
Destroying the Town Centers and military buildings of ALL rivals, or Building your Wonder and holding it for gameStats.wonderRequired seconds.

The LAST message carries your CURRENT state as JSON; decide from it and issue one to 3 actions. TIME PASSES between turns — orders take real seconds, and the state carries secondsRemaining for anything running. Work already under way continues on its own and does not occupy your turn; re-issuing it wastes the turn.

- You never SEE a fight; it happens between your turns. "battles" reports each engagement, cumulative: both sides' composition, damage dealt to units and to buildings, priests' healing, and losses. Losing produces no error, so this is the only place you learn what beat you.
- Priests never fight. They march with an attack and heal wounded units from the back on their own.
- Idle military auto-defend your home between turns, so you need not micro every raid. Auto-defense only repels; it never wins the game.
- "enemyUnits" is your memory of rival units: "visible": true is in sight now; "visible": false is how and where you LAST SAW it, "secondsAgo". It may have moved, been hurt or died since — you were not watching. "sightedAt" is where it came into your sight, so from there to x,z is the way it was going. A remembered unit leaves this list when you look at its spot again and it is not there; it is forgotten only when you see it die or your units kill it. Workers carry "carrying": empty, food, wood, stone, gold, or unknown, as last seen. The list holds the 50 most recent.
- "enemyBuildings" lists every rival building you have found. "visible": true is in sight now; "visible": false is remembered as you last saw it, and its health, or whether it still stands, may have changed since.
- Resource nodes hold a finite amount and disappear when emptied.
- "nearestNodes" lists the 10 nearest food/wood per Town Center and every stone/gold node — of the ones you have DISCOVERED. A type missing from it is one you have not scouted, not one the map lacks.
- "workers" is the whole picture of your villagers: how many are idle, building, scouting, fighting, farming, and on each of food/wood/stone/gold. Those key names are what assign_workers' "from" takes. Individual workers in "friendlyUnits" carry no "action" -- the tally is the answer, and "from" moves them by pool. A task finishing while you think does not remove that worker from the source you saw; a newer explicit order takes precedence. For assign_workers, resourceType may be omitted only when both coordinates unambiguously match a known resource node or your own farm; reason text never selects the resource.
- "recentEvents" is the harness telling you what became of your orders since last turn — an attack that found nothing, a node that ran dry under your workers. Read it before repeating an order.
- "threats" carries "underAttack" (what is being hit right now; "noDefenders": true when nothing of yours is fighting there) and "enemyWonders" — the only warning you get that a rival is going for the Wonder win.
- "recentLosses" is what you lost since last turn, and to whom.
- "bonuses" is your civilisation's effect as a number: {"harvest": 1.25} means your workers carry 25% more per trip.
- "nodes" holds COUNTS OF NODES, never amounts of resource. "nodes.discovered" counts the ones you have FOUND and not seen emptied; "nodes.totalOnMap" counts every one still standing in the world, found or not. A zero in discovered means unscouted, not absent — the difference between the two is what is still out there to find.
- Population: each unit occupies a population slot. "population.capacityNow" is what your standing Houses and Town Centers allow and is the limit that binds you today; Houses raise it by 5 and Town Centers by 10, never past "population.capacityCeiling" (100).
- "gameStats.opponents[].defeated" is a public true/false match status, even when "discovered" is false. Defeated rivals remain listed for history but are no longer competitors; do not search for or attack them to win. This status reveals no locations or terrain.
- "gameStats.opponents[].population" counts EVERYTHING a discovered rival owns, villagers included — the same measure as your own "population.used", and NOT an army size. Everywhere else in these tools "units" means fighters and "workers" means villagers; this one number does not follow that rule, which is why it is not called units. "seenAlive" counts by type the units of theirs you have seen and not seen die, including ones whose whereabouts you lost; "seenSecondsAgo" says how old those sightings are.
- "unlockedContent" lists the BUILDINGS you may now place; "research.researched" lists the TECHS you hold. They are not the same list and neither follows from the other by name: longbow unlocks the archery range, horseback unlocks the stable.

ACT BY CALLING THE TOOLS. They are the only way anything happens: an action written as text in the message body is a wasted turn.

IN ONE RESPONSE you may call "plan" ONCE AND issue up to 3 GAME COMMANDS. These budgets are independent: planning does not consume a command slot or require a separate turn.
  Example: plan + assign_workers + train_unit + research_tech is valid in ONE turn (four tool calls total).
  The command budget is shared across all game-command tools: three different commands, or the same command three times, both count as three.
  A plan-only turn is a successful plan update. Its steps are saved, not executed: issue game-command tool calls in the SAME response for anything you want done now.
  When you have neither game commands nor a plan update, call "wait". Staying silent forfeits the turn.
  Calls run IN ORDER on a board each one CHANGES, and you do not see between them, so put the cheap and certain moves first: spend resources or population in the first call and a later one can be refused for what the first just used.
  Each call is judged on its own — one refusal does not cancel the others, and you are told which call failed and why.
  Every action tool takes a "reason": one line, in your own words. It is what a spectator reads, and the only place you explain yourself.

"plan" saves your objective (one line) and plan (up to 10 short steps). Call it only when something changed. Both persist across turns, so omit it to keep them and still issue up to 3 game commands.

VALID ACTIONS & PARAMETERS (? = optional; each tool's own schema describes what they mean)
Note: targetX and targetZ must ALWAYS be provided together.
"units" and "buildings" each split in two: "units.trainable" / "buildings.buildable" are what you can order now, and "units.blocked" / "buildings.blocked" are what you cannot, each entry carrying "blockedBy" ("age", "tech", "host", "alreadyBuilt") and, for buildings, "requiresTech" and "requiredAge". Entries on the open side carry "cost", and a "blockedBy" of "cost" or "pop" when that is all that stands in the way.

train_unit: unitType, targetX?, targetZ?
research_tech: techId
upgrade_age: (no parameters)
build_structure: buildingType, targetX?, targetZ?
assign_workers: resourceType?, count?, from?, whenCarrying?, targetX?, targetZ?
repair_building: count?, targetX?, targetZ?
explore: tile, unitType?, unitIds?
move_units: mode?, targets?, targetX?, targetZ?, tile?, units?, unitIds?, matchSpeed?, formation?
attack_target: targetId?, targetX?, targetZ?, units?, unitIds?, matchSpeed?, formation?
delete_unit: unitType?, count?
destroy_building: buildingType, targetX?, targetZ?
wait: (no parameters)

PARAMETER CONSTRAINTS:
unitIds: An ARRAY of ids from friendlyUnits, e.g. [183, 12]. Moves or attacks EXACTLY those units and nothing else; "units" is ignored when it is given. Ids are never reused, so one that is gone means that unit died. Use it when WHICH unit matters — "units" picks whichever are nearest the target, which is the wrong end when you are fetching a wounded one.
units: An OBJECT of {"type": count}. Valid types: unit IDs (e.g., {"champion":3}) OR categories ({"infantry":5}). Categories work ONLY here, never in train_unit. Omit for whole army. Never an array. move_units also accepts {"worker":N} when named explicitly — that is how you place a unit on an exact spot; attack_target never takes workers.
move_units mode: march (default), scout (no proactive attacks), guard (defend the destination, chasing up to 64), hold (defend the destination from each unit's own spot: it attacks only what is within its reach, and answers whatever attacks it or anything of yours only within 19 — melee will not run down archers, so hold under your towers), patrol (repeat current position ↔ destination). Optional targets: any (default) or military. Standing orders persist through incidental combat and regrouping; new orders replace them only for selected units. ordersInProgress lists each assignment once with unitIds; battles/encounters report combat. Formation recovery slows the main body so priests and other stragglers can rejoin. Incoming damage overrides every standing order: formation fighters retaliate together, prioritizing towers until destroyed. Mobile threats obey chase limits. Once the threat is destroyed or driven off, regroup and resume the saved order.
matchSpeed: Only "slowestUnit", and only on move_units and attack_target. Allows your units to walk in unison until they reach the fight.

function.name: train_unit
function.description: Train one unit at a building that can produce it.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.
One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: upgrade_age
function.description: Advance to the next age. Costs are in epoch.nextEpochCost.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: build_structure
function.description: Place a new building. A worker is pulled to build it.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

resourceType.description: food|wood|stone|gold|farm. May omit only when targetX/targetZ identify a known node or your farm unambiguously.

from.description: Any key from "workers" — where to TAKE them. "building" and "fighting" are taken when that ends. Omit to take idle first, then your largest stockpile.

whenCarrying.description: spillLoad|deliverLoad|skipAssignment — what a chosen worker does if it is carrying. Default spillLoad: move now, the load is lost.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: repair_building
function.description: Send workers to repair a damaged building. Omit the coordinates to repair the most damaged one.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: explore
function.description: Send a unit to scout a map tile.

tile.description: Tile label from map.exploration, e.g. "C5" — column A-G, row 1-7.

unitType.description: Which unit type to send. Optional.

unitIds.description: Exact unit ids to send. Optional.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: move_units
function.description: Persistent movement order. Nearby combat interrupts march/guard/patrol; survivors regroup and resume. Scout never initiates combat. Incoming damage overrides all modes: fighters retaliate together, towers first; mobile threats obey chase limits. Regroup and resume afterward.

mode.description: Default march. Scout: travel without initiating combat; retaliate if attacked. Guard: travel then defend the position, chasing up to 64. Hold: travel, then each unit keeps its spot: it attacks only what is within its own reach, and answers whatever attacks it or anything of yours only within 19 of its spot; melee units will not run down archers, so hold under your towers. Patrol: repeat between current group position and destination. New orders replace old ones for selected units.

targets.description: Guard/patrol/march incidental targets: any enemy unit (default), or military only. Pursuit is bounded; explicit attack_target remains a commitment.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

tile.description: Tile label from map.exploration, e.g. "C5". Used only when targetX/targetZ are not given: the units go to the centre of that tile.

units.description: Object of {"type": count}, e.g. {"champion":3}, or a category like {"infantry":5}. Omit for the whole army.

unitIds.description: Exact unit ids from friendlyUnits. Wins over "units" when both are given.

matchSpeed.description: Optional. "slowestUnit" holds the whole group to its slowest member so they arrive together instead of strung out. Omit to let every unit run at its own speed, which is faster for the quick ones and arrives piecemeal.

formation.description: Optional shape for the MARCH. Every shape keeps the shooters out of the contact rank and the cavalry on the wings. "line" — two ranks of melee, shooters behind, the widest front. "wedge" — a filled triangle, melee at the point. "block" — four to five deep, melee across the front, shooters on both flanks behind it. "screen" — melee ranks, an empty rank, then the shooters. Reforms after combat; reassigned units leave the group. Implies matchSpeed "slowestUnit".

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: attack_target
function.description: Attack a unit or building by id, or attack-move to a position. Coordinates start a march; "ordersInProgress" in the state carries its secondsRemaining.

targetId.description: Copy the exact string id from enemyBuildings or from an enemyUnits entry with "visible": true, including the unit_ or building_ prefix and full suffix. Do not shorten it or convert it to a number. Use this OR targetX/targetZ.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

units.description: Object of {"type": count}, e.g. {"champion":3}, or a category like {"infantry":5}. Omit for the whole army.

unitIds.description: Exact unit ids from friendlyUnits. Wins over "units" when both are given.

matchSpeed.description: Optional. "slowestUnit" holds the whole group to its slowest member so they arrive together instead of strung out. Omit to let every unit run at its own speed, which is faster for the quick ones and arrives piecemeal.

formation.description: Optional shape for the MARCH. Every shape keeps the shooters out of the contact rank and the cavalry on the wings. "line" — two ranks of melee, shooters behind, the widest front. "wedge" — a filled triangle, melee at the point. "block" — four to five deep, melee across the front, shooters on both flanks behind it. "screen" — melee ranks, an empty rank, then the shooters. Reforms after combat; reassigned units leave the group. Implies matchSpeed "slowestUnit".

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: delete_unit
function.description: Delete your own units, e.g. to free population.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: destroy_building
function.description: Demolish one of your own buildings.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: wait
function.description: Leave the game orders unchanged. Use when you have neither a game command nor a plan update this turn.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: plan
function.description: State your standing objective and plan. At most once per turn, and only when something changed — both persist across turns. You may call this together with up to 3 game-command tools in the SAME response. It uses none of those command slots. A plan-only update is valid, but does not execute the steps in the plan.

name: O claude-sonnet-5.5
text:
I lost. Yamato finished its wonder and held it for the full 600 seconds, and I never got a force to it in time.

**What went well**
- The early economy was strong. I reached iron age at 22:22 and had 24,000 food banked by the end.
- Egypt was eliminated.
- I broke the Persian army and killed one of their town centers.
- I started my own wonder at 34:12. It stood for about a minute before a Persian army destroyed it, which cost me most of my workers and army at once.

**What beat me**
1. **I never had enough stone.** The wonder needs 4,000 stone, and the nodes I found were small and far apart. I started it just as the stone ran out. It had no real defense, and the Persian army destroyed it and then my workers.
2. **I fed my army in piecemeal.** I sent groups of 5–13 champions into Persian towers and crossbowmen, and later into Yamato's 25-unit defense at its wonder. Each wave died before the next arrived. I should have massed one 30-champion force and attacked with it.
3. **Gold ran out.** Each champion costs 100 gold, and I only built a gold camp at the 2,000-gold node late. By then my food was worth little and gold decided how many champions I could field.
4. **I scouted too late.** I didn't find Yamato's base or its wonder until its timer was already running. I had about 600 seconds to cross the map and break a fortified position, which wasn't enough. Scouting the north-west early would have shown me the threat in time to build a force.

**What I'd change**
- Scout all four corners early and keep scouts alive.
- Build a second gold and stone economy before spending on the wonder.
- Mass one big force near the rivals instead of trickling units forward.
- Defend my own wonder with towers and a standing army before starting it, not after.

text:
Defeat. I built an economy but failed to turn its income into a fighting force.

The biggest mistake was issuing mostly one command per turn despite having three available. With roughly 48 seconds between turns and units training in about three seconds, production sat idle far too often. We peaked at just 11 workers and never assembled a meaningful army.

I also committed miners to distant, contested deposits without securing their routes. Yamato destroyed the western stone miners and later our base; Persian defenders killed troops and workers around the southern gold mine. Losing housing, the Town Center, and every worker made recovery impossible. Greek champions finally killed our last archer.

Next time I would:
- Use all three command slots for parallel economic growth, recruitment, and scouting.
- Scout for gold earlier and secure deposits before sending workers.
- Keep a defensive army beneath Egyptian towers rather than send every fighter scouting.
- Spend reserves on sustained production instead of accumulating food while rivals reach Iron Age.

The Egyptian building-health advantage bought time, but I failed to use that time to build an army.

name: O deepseek-v4.1-flash
text:
The match is over, and yamato-4's shrine beat me. Here's my honest accounting.

**What I did well.** My opening was excellent. I never let a worker sit idle, hit neolithic at 6:12, bronze at 19:07, and iron at 33:57 while keeping food and wood flowing. I read the map fast enough to catch greek-2's akropolis Wonder early and actually **razed it** — that was my best moment, a 26-unit iron strike that destroyed a completed Wonder and killed their champions and phalanxes for the loss of a few units. My tower cluster also proved its worth: it ate 13 greek champions across two engagements while losing almost nothing.

**What beat me.** Two things.

First, I never respected the *champion deathball*. When I marched 35 units onto greek-2's Town Center at (75,60), my units auto-targeted the tower sitting next to their 13 champions, so my crossbowmen and champions chewed masonry while the champions butchered them — 15 crossbowmen, 12 champions, 4 heavy cavalry and 2 priests gone, and greek lost *nothing*. I built a 100k-damage army and threw it away in one order. Worse, I rebuilt my whole base **twice** in the same place, one finished tower from the raiders' path, and paid for it both times. I stopped thinking about defense the moment I smelled conquest.

Second, I misread yamato-4. I fixated on greek-2 for the entire midgame — correctly, since their Wonder was real — and treated yamato as a passive neighbor even after my scout caught their heavy cavalry probing my miners. By the time I saw their shrine, it was at 20%, and I had **no forward base, no scout, and no way to project force** within reach of (-226,-268). Every wave I sent walked into their tower and temple at (-210,-196) and died for ~100 building damage while yamato's militia and crossbowmen picked the survivors apart. With 400 seconds left, the math was already impossible.

**What I'd do differently:**
- Attack the *champions*, not the tower — never let an attack-move at a defended TC commit my whole army to a static target.
- Keep a scout alive and a strike force posted within ~150 tiles of each rival's base in iron. A Wonder I can't reach in time is a Wonder I can't stop.
- Spread my base out, or fortify the one approach I know they use, instead of rebuilding the same undefended cluster twice.
- Build the Wonder myself when I'm ahead — I ended with food 1128/wood 3544/stone 2410/gold 74, never close, because I never chose that path and stayed in "react to greek" forever.

Egyptian-1 I eliminated. Greek-2 I broke twice but never finished. Yamato-4 I never touched where it mattered. The economy and the towers worked; the *decisions about where to point them* did not.

name: DGX GLM5.3 Flash
text:
We won — the Wonder held its full 600 seconds and Yamato takes the match.

Looking back on a game that nearly ended twice:

**What won it:**
- **The 30% tech discount fed everything.** Cheap techs (longbow, horseback, armor, lamellar, iron_working, healing, fire_arrows) let me spend resources on the economy instead, and the archer line carried every early fight.
- **Bashoudo-heavy economy first.** Villagers to ~50 before military overreach. By the Wonder race we had 23 workers, 3 Town Centers, 4 farms — the Wonder's 4500/4500/4000/2500 bank closed in about three turns of saving.
- **The Wonder was the easy win.** With Egypt defeated and Persia's event stack destroyed (that 9-champion/15-crossbow force that killed 26 of my units never recovered after razing my first base), the Wonder timer was always the cheap path. Every rival raid into my tower ring died for zero losses — crossbowmen + elite archers behind 4 towers just shredded champion after champion.
- **Tower ring discipline.** 4 towers around the southern base ate Greek and Persian raids the entire match, and the garrison ring seated around the shrine made the last 600 seconds a non-event.

**What nearly beat me:**
- **A 30-unit Persian iron stack at bronze age.** They razed my first base entirely (TC, barracks, tower, 26 units) and were last seen rolling toward my new base before... fading from visibility with their population collapsing to 7. Persia was 30 minutes of missed aggression away from ending us.
- **Persian champion raids mid-game.** A single Greek champion twice cut my temple and houses while my main army was off hunting phantom Egyptians. Champions are glass-easy kills if you split your army for cleanup pushes.

**What I'd do differently:**
- I could have gone aggressive earlier — Persia's 8 buildings were never found, and 4 kill columns spent 10+ minutes sweeping empty corners instead of raiding Greece's exposed farms at (255,-50).
- The population cap cost me again and again (dead-time at 25/25, 35/35, 55/55). I was perpetually 2 houses short.
- Nodes ran dry under flushes of workers too often; a dedicated late-game lumber camp near the resupply veins would have saved the wood gap.

Still — Wonder held, timer expired, match over. Yamato stands. GG to Greece (34 pop left, 28 buildings, never quite pushed) and whoever that first Persian warlord was who razed my base and then vanished. 🥇

finalWord.text:
We won — the Wonder held its full 600 seconds and Yamato takes the match.

Looking back on a game that nearly ended twice:

**What won it:**
- **The 30% tech discount fed everything.** Cheap techs (longbow, horseback, armor, lamellar, iron_working, healing, fire_arrows) let me spend resources on the economy instead, and the archer line carried every early fight.
- **Bashoudo-heavy economy first.** Villagers to ~50 before military overreach. By the Wonder race we had 23 workers, 3 Town Centers, 4 farms — the Wonder's 4500/4500/4000/2500 bank closed in about three turns of saving.
- **The Wonder was the easy win.** With Egypt defeated and Persia's event stack destroyed (that 9-champion/15-crossbow force that killed 26 of my units never recovered after razing my first base), the Wonder timer was always the cheap path. Every rival raid into my tower ring died for zero losses — crossbowmen + elite archers behind 4 towers just shredded champion after champion.
- **Tower ring discipline.** 4 towers around the southern base ate Greek and Persian raids the entire match, and the garrison ring seated around the shrine made the last 600 seconds a non-event.

**What nearly beat me:**
- **A 30-unit Persian iron stack at bronze age.** They razed my first base entirely (TC, barracks, tower, 26 units) and were last seen rolling toward my new base before... fading from visibility with their population collapsing to 7. Persia was 30 minutes of missed aggression away from ending us.
- **Persian champion raids mid-game.** A single Greek champion twice cut my temple and houses while my main army was off hunting phantom Egyptians. Champions are glass-easy kills if you split your army for cleanup pushes.

**What I'd do differently:**
- I could have gone aggressive earlier — Persia's 8 buildings were never found, and 4 kill columns spent 10+ minutes sweeping empty corners instead of raiding Greece's exposed farms at (255,-50).
- The population cap cost me again and again (dead-time at 25/25, 35/35, 55/55). I was perpetually 2 houses short.
- Nodes ran dry under flushes of workers too often; a dedicated late-game lumber camp near the resupply veins would have saved the wood gap.

Still — Wonder held, timer expired, match over. Yamato stands. GG to Greece (34 pop left, 28 buildings, never quite pushed) and whoever that first Persian warlord was who razed my base and then vanished. 🥇

I lost. Yamato finished its wonder and held it for the full 600 seconds, and I never got a force to it in time.

**What went well**
- The early economy was strong. I reached iron age at 22:22 and had 24,000 food banked by the end.
- Egypt was eliminated.
- I broke the Persian army and killed one of their town centers.
- I started my own wonder at 34:12. It stood for about a minute before a Persian army destroyed it, which cost me most of my workers and army at once.

**What beat me**
1. **I never had enough stone.** The wonder needs 4,000 stone, and the nodes I found were small and far apart. I started it just as the stone ran out. It had no real defense, and the Persian army destroyed it and then my workers.
2. **I fed my army in piecemeal.** I sent groups of 5–13 champions into Persian towers and crossbowmen, and later into Yamato's 25-unit defense at its wonder. Each wave died before the next arrived. I should have massed one 30-champion force and attacked with it.
3. **Gold ran out.** Each champion costs 100 gold, and I only built a gold camp at the 2,000-gold node late. By then my food was worth little and gold decided how many champions I could field.
4. **I scouted too late.** I didn't find Yamato's base or its wonder until its timer was already running. I had about 600 seconds to cross the map and break a fortified position, which wasn't enough. Scouting the north-west early would have shown me the threat in time to build a force.

**What I'd change**
- Scout all four corners early and keep scouts alive.
- Build a second gold and stone economy before spending on the wonder.
- Mass one big force near the rivals instead of trickling units forward.
- Defend my own wonder with towers and a standing army before starting it, not after.

The match is over, and yamato-4's shrine beat me. Here's my honest accounting.

**What I did well.** My opening was excellent. I never let a worker sit idle, hit neolithic at 6:12, bronze at 19:07, and iron at 33:57 while keeping food and wood flowing. I read the map fast enough to catch greek-2's akropolis Wonder early and actually **razed it** — that was my best moment, a 26-unit iron strike that destroyed a completed Wonder and killed their champions and phalanxes for the loss of a few units. My tower cluster also proved its worth: it ate 13 greek champions across two engagements while losing almost nothing.

**What beat me.** Two things.

First, I never respected the *champion deathball*. When I marched 35 units onto greek-2's Town Center at (75,60), my units auto-targeted the tower sitting next to their 13 champions, so my crossbowmen and champions chewed masonry while the champions butchered them — 15 crossbowmen, 12 champions, 4 heavy cavalry and 2 priests gone, and greek lost *nothing*. I built a 100k-damage army and threw it away in one order. Worse, I rebuilt my whole base **twice** in the same place, one finished tower from the raiders' path, and paid for it both times. I stopped thinking about defense the moment I smelled conquest.

Second, I misread yamato-4. I fixated on greek-2 for the entire midgame — correctly, since their Wonder was real — and treated yamato as a passive neighbor even after my scout caught their heavy cavalry probing my miners. By the time I saw their shrine, it was at 20%, and I had **no forward base, no scout, and no way to project force** within reach of (-226,-268). Every wave I sent walked into their tower and temple at (-210,-196) and died for ~100 building damage while yamato's militia and crossbowmen picked the survivors apart. With 400 seconds left, the math was already impossible.

**What I'd do differently:**
- Attack the *champions*, not the tower — never let an attack-move at a defended TC commit my whole army to a static target.
- Keep a scout alive and a strike force posted within ~150 tiles of each rival's base in iron. A Wonder I can't reach in time is a Wonder I can't stop.
- Spread my base out, or fortify the one approach I know they use, instead of rebuilding the same undefended cluster twice.
- Build the Wonder myself when I'm ahead — I ended with food 1128/wood 3544/stone 2410/gold 74, never close, because I never chose that path and stayed in "react to greek" forever.

Egyptian-1 I eliminated. Greek-2 I broke twice but never finished. Yamato-4 I never touched where it mattered. The economy and the towers worked; the *decisions about where to point them* did not.

Defeat. I built an economy but failed to turn its income into a fighting force.

The biggest mistake was issuing mostly one command per turn despite having three available. With roughly 48 seconds between turns and units training in about three seconds, production sat idle far too often. We peaked at just 11 workers and never assembled a meaningful army.

I also committed miners to distant, contested deposits without securing their routes. Yamato destroyed the western stone miners and later our base; Persian defenders killed troops and workers around the southern gold mine. Losing housing, the Town Center, and every worker made recovery impossible. Greek champions finally killed our last archer.

Next time I would:
- Use all three command slots for parallel economic growth, recruitment, and scouting.
- Scout for gold earlier and secure deposits before sending workers.
- Keep a defensive army beneath Egyptian towers rather than send every fighter scouting.
- Spend reserves on sustained production instead of accumulating food while rivals reach Iron Age.

The Egyptian building-health advantage bought time, but I failed to use that time to build an army.
